question: In the 2022 VetCompass life-table study of UK companion dogs, based on 30,563 dogs that died between January 2016 and July 2020, what was the estimated life expectancy at age 0 for all dogs?

evidence.title: Life tables of annual life expectancy and mortality for companion dogs in the United Kingdom.
evidence.quote: Among 30,563 dogs that died between 1st January 2016 and 31st July 2020, life expectancy at age 0 was 11.23 [95% confidence interval (CI): 11.19-11.27] years.

question: In the 2023 study that generated life expectancy tables for dogs and cats from Banfield Pet Hospital clinical records in the USA (survey years 2013-2019), what was the life expectancy at birth for all dogs?

evidence.title: Life expectancy tables for dogs and cats derived from clinical data.
evidence.quote: LE at birth (LE<sub>birth</sub>) was 12.69 years (95% CI: 12.68-12.70) for all dogs, 12.71 years (12.67-12.76) for mixed-breed dogs, 11.18 years (11.16-11.20) for cats, and 11.12 (11.09-11.14) for mixed-breed cats.

question: In the 2015 life table constructed from 299,555 dogs insured in Japan between April 2010 and March 2011, what was the overall life expectancy of dogs?

evidence.title: A current life table and causes of death for insured dogs in Japan.
evidence.quote: The life expectancies and causes of death were evaluated in 299,555 dogs insured in Japan between 1 April 2010 and 31 March 2011, of which 4169 dogs died during this period. The overall life expectancy of dogs was 13.7 years.

question: In the analysis of 137,469 dogs that died in Switzerland between 2016 and 2020 (Amicus national database), what was the mean life expectancy of brachycephalic dogs, and how much shorter was it than that of mesocephalic and dolichocephalic dogs?
answer: 9.8 years; 2.1 years less than mesocephalic dogs and 1.7 years less than dolichocephalic dogs.

evidence.title: [Life expectancy of mesocephalic, dolichocephalic and brachycephalic dog breeds in Switzerland].
evidence.quote: The mean life expectancy of brachycephalic dogs was 9,8 years, i.e., 2,1 and 1,7 years less than mesocephalic and dolichocephalic dogs, respectively.

notes: Decimal commas in the source (9,8; 2,1; 1,7) correspond to 9.8, 2.1 and 1.7 years.

question: In the 2018 owner-survey study of mortality in 5,663 deceased UK Kennel Club-registered dogs, which breeds had the longest and the shortest median longevity, and what were the values?
answer: Longest: West Highland Terrier (12.71 years); shortest: Dobermann Pinscher (7.67 years). Overall median age at death was 10.33 years.

evidence.title: Longevity and mortality in Kennel Club registered dog breeds in the UK in 2014.
evidence.quote: Overall median age at death was 10.33 years (interquartile range: 7.17-12.83 years). Breeds varied widely in median longevity overall from the West Highland Terrier (12.71 years) to the Dobermann Pinscher (7.67 years).

question: In the 2015 life table of dogs insured in Japan, life expectancy was reported for five body-weight groups (<5 kg, 5-10 kg, 10-20 kg, 20-40 kg and >=40 kg). Which group had the highest life expectancy, and what was its value?
answer: The 5-10 kg group, at 14.2 years; the <5 kg group (13.8 years) was the exception to the decline of life expectancy with increasing body weight.

evidence.title: A current life table and causes of death for insured dogs in Japan.
evidence.quote: The life expectancy was 13.8 years in the <5 kg body weight group, 14.2 years in the 5-10 kg body weight group, 13.6 years in the 10-20 kg body weight group, 12.5 years in the 20-40 kg body weight group and 10.6 years in the ≥40 kg body weight group. As body weight increases, life expectancy tended to decrease except in the <5 kg body weight group.

question: In the 2013 analysis that fitted mortality hazard models to death data from 74 dog breeds to decompose the size-lifespan trade-off, which mortality component was identified as the driving force behind the shorter lifespan of large dogs, and was body size clearly correlated with the onset of senescence?
answer: A strong positive relationship between body size and aging rate (large dogs die young mainly because they age quickly); no clear correlation between body size and onset of senescence was found, and baseline hazard was only slightly higher in large dogs.

evidence.title: The size-life span trade-off decomposed: why large dogs die young.
evidence.quote: We did not find a clear correlation between body size and the onset of senescence. The baseline hazard is slightly higher in large dogs, but the driving force behind the trade-off between size and life span is apparently a strong positive relationship between size and aging rate.

question: In the 2020 study of 20,970 privately owned dogs seen at three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States, by how much shorter were the median survival times of breeds in the "Mountain" ancestral group compared with other purebred dog groups, and did the difference persist after correcting for body size?
answer: 3.5-4.6 years shorter; yes, the difference remained significant even when correcting for body size.

evidence.title: Lifespan of companion dogs seen in three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States.
evidence.quote: We also found that dog breeds belonging to the "Mountain" ancestral group had median survival times that were 3.5-4.6 years shorter than other purebred dog groups, which remained significant even when correcting for body size.

question: In the 2013 analysis of 5,095 confirmed deaths among 102,609 owned dogs attending first-opinion veterinary practices in central and southeast England, by how many years did the longevity of crossbred dogs exceed that of purebred dogs in multivariable modelling, and what was the direction of the association between bodyweight and longevity?
answer: Crossbred dogs outlived purebreds by 1.2 years (95% CI 0.9-1.4; P<0.001); increasing bodyweight was negatively correlated with longevity.

evidence.title: Longevity and mortality of owned dogs in England.
evidence.quote: The results of multivariable modelling indicated that longevity in crossbred dogs exceeded purebred dogs by 1.2 years (95% confidence interval 0.9-1.4; P<0.001) and that increasing bodyweight was negatively correlated with longevity.

question: According to the 2024 review that examined dog aging and mortality studies spanning about 40 years (1981 to 2023) to assess how average dog lifespan is reported, has the median lifespan of domesticated dogs recently decreased, as claimed in the popular press?
answer: No. The review concluded that median lifespan has not recently decreased but rather has increased steadily over that time frame.

evidence.title: How can we achieve more accurate reporting of average dog lifespan?
evidence.quote: However, in examining several different kinds of dog aging and mortality studies covering a span of about 40 years (1981 to 2023), it seems apparent that the median lifespan of domesticated dogs has not recently decreased, as has been reported in the popular press, but rather has increased steadily over that time frame.

question: In the 2023 Banfield study that generated life expectancy tables for dogs and cats from clinical records of more than 1,000 US hospitals, which life-table method was used, and how were survivors defined for each survey year?
answer: Sullivan's method; survivors were animals with no death date recorded in that survey year who were confirmed living by a veterinary visit in a subsequent year.

evidence.title: Life expectancy tables for dogs and cats derived from clinical data.
evidence.quote: Using Sullivan's method, LE tables were generated across survey years 2013-2019, by survey year, and for subpopulations defined by sex, adult body size group (purebred dogs only: toy, small, medium, large and giant), and median body condition score (BCS) over life. The deceased population for each survey year comprised animals with a recorded date of death in that year; survivors had no death date in that year and were confirmed living by a veterinary visit in a subsequent year.

question: In the 2025 life-table study of companion dogs from six veterinary hospitals in Seoul, South Korea, life expectancy at age 1 was higher than at age 0. What were the two life expectancy values, and what pattern of mortality explains the difference?
answer: 9.390 years at age 0 versus 10.123 years at age 1; the probability of dying between ages 0 and 1 was 0.161, whereas from age 1 to age 10 the probability of dying at each age was below 0.1.

evidence.title: Life expectancy and survival analysis for companion dogs and cats in Seoul, South Korea.
evidence.quote: In the life tables created for the dog and cat study populations, the life expectancy at age 0 was 9.390 years in dogs and 5.384 in cats. The probability of a dog dying between the ages of 0 and 1 year was 0.161. After age 1 until age 10, the probability of dying at each age was <0.1, so the dog's life expectancy was higher at age 1 (10.123 years) than at age 0 (9.390 years).

question: In the 2024 UK study of 584,734 dogs (284,734 deceased) that estimated Kaplan-Meier median survival separately for purebred and crossbred dogs, what were the two median survival estimates, and which group lived longer?
answer: Purebreds 12.7 years versus crossbreds 12.0 years; purebreds lived longer (crossbred hazard ratio 1.1, p<0.001).

evidence.title: Longevity of companion dog breeds: those at risk from early death.
evidence.quote: Median survival for pure breeds was 12.7 years (12.6-12.7, n = 473,681, events = 212,289), whilst median survival for crossbreds was 12.0 years (12.0-12.1, n = 111,053, events = 72,445, HR 1.1, 1.1-1.1, p < 0.001).

notes: Notable because it runs counter to the usual crossbred longevity advantage reported in other datasets (e.g. the 2013 England VetCompass analysis).

question: Both the 2022 VetCompass life-table study of UK companion dogs and the 2024 study of life expectancy at birth using Portugal's national registry (278,116 dogs) identified the breed with the lowest life expectancy at birth. Which breed was it in each study, and what were the two estimates?
answer: French Bulldog in both studies: 4.53 years (95% CI 4.14-5.01) in the UK and 6.27 years in Portugal.

evidence.title: Life tables of annual life expectancy and mortality for companion dogs in the United Kingdom.
evidence.quote: Jack Russell Terrier (12.72 years; 95% CI: 12.53-12.90) and French Bulldog (4.53 years; 95% CI: 4.14-5.01) had the longest and shortest life expectancy at age 0, respectively.

evidence.title: Investigating the Life Expectancy at Birth of Companion Dogs in Portugal Using Official National Registry Data.
evidence.quote: The analysis of life expectancy at birth for the 20 most common non-Portuguese breeds and 10 Portuguese breeds revealed that Yorkshire Terriers had the highest life expectancy (10.89 years) and French Bulldogs the lowest (6.27 years).

notes: The Portuguese full text (Table 2 section) reports 6.29 years for the French Bulldog and 11.7 years for the Yorkshire Terrier, which differs slightly from the abstract values; the gold answer follows the abstract.
